x: The Attorney General's office is created by Article 76. Article 88 gives him rights in Parliament, Article 105(4) privileges, and Article 165 creates the State Advocate General.
t: Separate the creating Article (76) from related ones.

x: B is incorrect: the Attorney General's remuneration is fixed by the President, not Parliament. He holds office during the President's pleasure and can be removed at any time.
t: Recall that the President controls both pay and tenure.

x: Both are true and R explains A: since the Attorney General serves during the President's pleasure, the Constitution gives him no fixed term.
t: Ask whether 'pleasure' explains the lack of tenure.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts in India, and that right attaches to his official duties.
t: Check whether R states the condition attached to A.

x: Both are true: the Attorney General is a constitutional post under Article 76, while the Solicitor General is a statutory, non-constitutional post that assists him.
t: Separate constitutional from statutory law officers.

x: I, III and IV are correct: the Attorney General can speak in either House, be named to committees and enjoys MPs' privileges (Article 105(4)). II is wrong: he cannot vote.
t: Speak yes, vote no.

x: Attorney General – Article 76; Advocate General – Article 165; Solicitor General – statutory post; the Attorney General is appointed by the President.
t: Match each law officer to its legal basis.

x: Attorney General – highest law officer of India; serves the Union; Advocate General – serves the State Government; Solicitor General – assists the Attorney General.
t: Match each officer to his level and role.

x: Both are true: the Attorney General resigns to the President and, by convention, quits when the Council of Ministers changes.
t: Recall the convention of resigning with the government.

x: All four are correct: the Attorney General needs the qualifications of a Supreme Court judge — an Indian citizen who was a High Court judge for 5 years, or a High Court advocate for 10 years, or an eminent jurist in the President's opinion.
t: Recall the Supreme Court judge qualifications.

x: C is incorrect: the Attorney General performs legal duties referred by the President, not by a Governor (the State's legal adviser is the Advocate General).
t: Check the authority named in each option.

x: Advocate General – appointed by the Governor and holds office at his pleasure; Solicitor General – appointed by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet, with a fixed term.
t: Separate the State officer from the Union officer.

x: Both are true: the Advocate General can speak in the State Legislature under Article 177, while the Solicitor General has no right to address Parliament.
t: Compare law officers' rights in legislatures.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 88 gives the Attorney General the right to speak and take part in either House and in joint sittings (without vote).
t: Check whether R is the source of A.

x: All five are correct: the Solicitor General and Additional SGs are non-constitutional posts that assist the Attorney General, who is not in the Cabinet, not a full-time government servant, and may do private practice within restrictions.
t: Recall the Attorney General's unusual status.

x: The CAG is in Part V, Chapter V, Articles 148–151. Part XII is finance, and Chapter VI is not the CAG chapter.
t: Recall Part V Chapter V for the CAG.

x: B is incorrect: the CAG is an independent constitutional authority (Article 148), not a statutory body under the Finance Ministry. He heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department and is the 'guardian of the public purse'.
t: Check constitutional vs statutory status.

x: Both are true: Ambedkar called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution, and the CAG, Supreme Court, UPSC and Election Commission are seen as the four bulwarks of democracy.
t: Recall how the CAG is described.

x: The CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act was passed in 1971. 1976 is the year accounting was separated from audit.
t: Separate 1971 (Act) from 1976 (reform).

x: The President appoints the CAG by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 148(1)) — not the PM, Finance Minister or PAC.
t: Recall the 'warrant under hand and seal'.

x: The CAG serves six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. 62 is the State PSC retirement age, a common distractor.
t: Recall '6 years or 65'.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the CAG is removed like a Supreme Court judge — by the President on an address of both Houses passed by special majority for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.
t: Check whether R describes the procedure in A.

x: A is incorrect: under Article 148(4) the CAG cannot hold any further office under either the Union or any State after retirement.
t: Remember the post-retirement bar is total.

x: A is true: Parliament fixes the CAG's salary and service conditions (Article 148(3), Second Schedule). B is false: they cannot be changed to his disadvantage after appointment.
t: Recall the protection of service conditions.

x: Article 148 – the CAG; 149 – duties and powers; 150 – form of accounts; 151 – audit reports.
t: Recall Articles 148–151 in order.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the President laying the report before Parliament is a later step; it does not explain why the report goes to the President first.
t: A next step does not explain the first step.

x: I, II and III are correct: the CAG audits Consolidated Fund spending, Contingency Funds and Public Accounts, and stores, stocks and government companies. IV is wrong: he does not control treasury issues day to day.
t: The Indian CAG audits; he does not control withdrawals.

x: Two: auditing government companies and performance audits are CAG functions. He cannot prosecute or control treasury withdrawals.
t: Separate audit functions from executive powers.

x: A performance audit checks the 3 Es: economy, efficiency and effectiveness of schemes and spending.
t: Recall the 3 Es.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the 1976 reform separated accounts from audit, so the Controller General of Accounts took over compiling Union accounts from 1 March 1976.
t: Ask whether the reform caused the change in A.

x: I, II and III are correct: the CAG cannot disallow expenditure, enforce recovery or prosecute. IV is wrong: he has no power to punish; he only reports to the legislature.
t: The CAG reports; he does not punish.

x: Union report – President; State report – Governor; for the PAC – 'friend, philosopher and guide'; final action – Parliament or State Legislature.
t: Match each step of audit follow-up.

x: The CAG is the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the Public Accounts Committee, helping it examine audit reports line by line. He is not its chairman.
t: Recall the PAC description.

x: Both are true and R explains A: under Article 150 the President prescribes the form of Union and State accounts, on the CAG's advice.
t: Check whether R states how A is done.

x: Under Article 151(2) a State audit report goes to the Governor, who lays it before the State Legislature.
t: State reports go to the Governor.

x: Under Article 149 the CAG audits receipts, expenditures, stores and accounts of the Union and States, so every item is an audit area (the same answer for each row).
t: A code with identical answers is possible.

x: I and II are correct: the CAG audits the Consolidated Funds of India, of the States and of UTs with legislatures. III is wrong because of the word 'only'.
t: Watch for 'only'.

x: The CAG audits manufacturing, trading and profit-and-loss accounts of government entities. He does not approve withdrawals, disallow expenditure or prosecute.
t: Pick the audit task, not an executive power.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the Indian CAG is only an Auditor General whose audit is after spending, so he does not control the issue of money from the treasury.
t: Ask whether post-audit explains no prior control.

x: Three are correct: the CAG stopped compiling Union accounts from 1 March 1976, still keeps most States' accounts, and the CGA compiles Union accounts. Statement 4 is wrong: the reform separated, not merged, the two functions.
t: Check the direction of the 1976 reform.

x: After 1976 the CAG still compiles and maintains the accounts of most States; Union accounts are handled by the Controller General of Accounts.
t: Separate Union accounts from State accounts.

x: A is incorrect: the CAG cannot enforce recovery of money. He can audit profit-and-loss accounts, stores and stocks and Public Account transactions.
t: Spot the enforcement power the CAG lacks.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the CAG helps the PAC by attending its meetings and assisting line by line in examining his reports.
t: Check whether R describes how the help is given.

x: Both are true: the CAG's administrative expenses, including salaries, allowances and pensions of him and his staff, are charged on the Consolidated Fund and so are not voted.
t: Charged expenditure is non-votable.

x: Both are true and R explains A: since the CAG has no day-to-day control over the exchequer, he cannot stop withdrawals in advance; he audits afterwards.
t: Ask whether lack of control explains A.

x: D is incorrect: the CAG only audits and reports; the final responsibility to act on his findings lies with Parliament (Union) or the State Legislature.
t: The CAG reports; the legislature acts.

x: Both are true and R explains A: the CAG cannot disallow spending because his constitutional job is to audit, not to control expenditure.
t: Ask whether his audit role explains the limit.

x: A is false: audit reports go first to the President or Governor, who lay them before the legislature. B is true: the CAG then helps the PAC examine them.
t: Trace the report's path before it reaches the PAC.

x: I, II and III are correct: the CAG audits government companies, stores and stocks, and trading accounts. IV is wrong: he cannot enforce recovery.
t: Remove the enforcement power.

x: Role in the PAC – friend, philosopher and guide; action on Union findings – Parliament; treasury – no day-to-day control; recovery – no power to enforce.
t: Match each item to the CAG's limits.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Article 148(1) read with Article 124(4) applies the Supreme Court judge's removal process, which ends with the President's order after Parliament's address.
t: Check whether R gives the legal basis of A.

x: All of these are in Article 148: appointment and oath, tenure and removal, the post-retirement bar and salary and charged expenses, each matching its own description.
t: Match each item to its description.

x: Both are true: the British CAG controls the issue of money from the treasury, whereas India's CAG is only an Auditor General without that control.
t: Contrast the British and Indian CAG.

x: The UPSC Chairman cannot take any further government job after retirement, whereas retired judges often head commissions and tribunals.
t: Compare post-retirement rules of the two offices.
